sections.title: Position and velocity change each other
teaching: A harmonic oscillator has two changing quantities, position x and velocity v. Position tells us where something is relative to its reference position. Velocity tells us how that position is changing. A dot above a quantity means its rate of change as time passes, using Isaac Newton’s notation. A positive rate makes the quantity increase, and a negative rate makes it decrease.

The two relationships are ẋ = v and v̇ = −x. The first says that velocity determines how position changes. The second says that position determines how velocity changes, with the sign reversed. A positive position makes velocity decrease, while a negative position makes velocity increase. Position and velocity therefore keep changing one another through a feedback loop.

sections.title: Read the sign of the change
teaching: When v is +5, ẋ is positive and position rises. When v is −5, ẋ is negative and position falls. These are statements about the direction of motion, not about whether the current position itself is positive or negative.

When x is +5, v̇ is negative and velocity goes down. When x is −5, v̇ is positive and velocity goes up. A velocity that goes up can move from a large negative value toward zero before becoming positive. Increasing velocity does not always mean moving faster in the same direction.

sections.title: Two different sign relationships
teaching: The relationship ẋ = v preserves the sign. Positive velocity makes position rise, and negative velocity makes position fall. The relationship v̇ = −x reverses the sign. Positive position makes velocity fall, and negative position makes velocity rise.

The quantity changed by v̇ is velocity. A positive position can therefore be associated with a decreasing velocity even while the object is still moving toward larger positions. Keeping the quantity and its rate separate makes the back-and-forth motion understandable.

sections.title: Follow the position–velocity cycle
teaching: Consider a positive position with zero velocity. Because x is positive, v̇ = −x makes velocity become negative. Negative velocity then makes x decrease. As x gets closer to zero, the change pushing velocity downward weakens, but the negative velocity still carries position through zero.

Once x is negative, v̇ becomes positive. Velocity rises toward zero and then becomes positive, so position turns around and rises. Positive velocity carries position back through zero. Positive x then starts reducing velocity again. These two simple relationships produce repeated motion rather than a single return to the reference position.

The hand-drawn position and velocity traces represent this continuing alternation. They are coordinated but do not peak together. Position can be at a turning point when velocity is zero, and velocity can still be nonzero when position passes through zero.

sections.title: A closed feedback loop
teaching: Position affects velocity, and velocity affects position. In the diagram, one arrow goes from X to V and the other returns from V to X. The arrows close the loop, so a change does not stop after one effect. It changes the other quantity, which changes the first quantity again.
The alternating high and low parts of the vibration trace are the result of this continuing interaction. Oscillation and vibration both refer to repeated back-and-forth change.

sections.title: Compression and rarefaction of air
teaching: A material slice of air contains particles whose distances change. During compression, the same particles move closer together and pressure is high. During rarefaction, they move farther apart and pressure is low. The dots keep the same size and the same particles remain in the slice. The change is in spacing, not in the number or size of particles.

The dashed circle marks the equilibrium size, and the highlighted orange pair tracks the distance between two particles. At equilibrium its distance is 100% of the equilibrium distance. During a compressed phase the percentage is below 100%, and during an expanded phase it is above 100%. For example, the inspected animation includes a compressed spacing near 60% and a rarefied spacing near 140%. The motion is deliberately exaggerated so the changing distances can be followed.

The slice repeatedly contracts through compression, expands through its equilibrium spacing, reaches rarefaction, and contracts again. A vibration in air is therefore a changing pattern of compression and rarefaction.

sections.title: Connect air motion to a cosine
teaching: The normalized expansion of the air slice is x = cos(phase). The vertical axis runs from −1 through 0 to +1, and the horizontal phase axis runs from 0 through π, 2π, 3π, 4π, 5π and 6π. Each interval of 2π is one complete cycle, so the graph contains three cycles.

At phase 0, x is +1 and the particles are farthest apart, giving maximum rarefaction. As the value falls toward zero, the expanded slice contracts toward its equilibrium size. Negative values mean compression, with x = −1 at phase π marking the closest spacing. The value then rises through zero and returns to +1 at 2π. The same sequence repeats from 2π to 4π and from 4π to 6π.

The moving point links a particular place on the curve to the particle spacing at that moment. The graph is an account of changing expansion, not a picture of particles travelling along a wavy path. The fixed dot sizes and dashed equilibrium circle make that distinction visible. Playback is slowed and the spatial motion is exaggerated.

sections.title: Vowels depend on tongue position
teaching: Vowel production changes the shape of the air space above the vocal folds. The tongue can be relatively high or low, and relatively toward the front or back of the mouth. High and low describe tongue height. Front and back describe the horizontal location of the tongue’s main raised region.

The vowel in dean occupies the high-front position in the comparison, and the vowel in dune occupies the high-back position. Dan supplies the low-front example and Don the low-back example. Done is the central example. These five MRI views compare different tongue shapes within the same overall vocal-tract space.
Changing tongue height and frontness changes where the air is squeezed and where it has more room. The physical shape of the vocal tract therefore changes with the vowel.

sections.title: Vowels combine more than one vibration
teaching: A vowel can contain a combination of vibrations rather than a single cosine. The illustrative /i/ model combines 1 Hz and 4 Hz components with equal amplitudes, written x(t) = cos(2πt) + cos(8πt). The illustrative /a/ model combines 2 Hz and 3 Hz components, written x(t) = cos(4πt) + cos(6πt). These deliberately slow model frequencies make the combination visible.

Both graphs plot x against signal time from 0 to 3 seconds, with the displayed vertical scale extending from −2 to +2. Both combinations begin at +2 because both component vibrations begin together at their positive maxima. They return to that same maximum once per second, yet their motion within each second differs because their component frequencies differ.

The /i/ curve contains relatively rapid small fluctuations superimposed on a slower rise and fall. The /a/ curve has a different arrangement of deep troughs and small humps between its large positive peaks. The two orange moving points can have different signs at the same time, so one air slice can be compressed while the other is rarefied. Positive x marks rarefaction and negative x marks compression.

The particle diagrams follow the combined value, so equal starting values do not mean identical motion throughout the cycle. The difference between the two patterns comes from which frequencies are combined. The demonstration uses equal component amplitudes and quarter-speed playback, rather than claiming that these low numbers are measured human vowel formants.

sections.title: Two vibrating parts of speech
teaching: Speaking involves vibration of the vocal folds and vibration of the air in the vocal tract. These are two physically different things. The folds are moving tissue, while the air is undergoing changing compression and rarefaction. An explanation of speech must account for both.

sections.title: Economic cycles around a growth trend
teaching: The business-cycle graph places time on the horizontal axis and level of real output on the vertical axis. Output rises toward a peak, falls during recession, reaches a trough, and rises again during recovery. Those rises and falls form a repeating pattern.

The sloping trend line represents growth across time. The economic cycle moves above and below that changing trend, so repeated fluctuation can coexist with an overall increase. Oscillation therefore does not require the long-term baseline to remain horizontal.

sections.title: Atoms, shell pictures and wave modes
teaching: Oscillatory ideas also enter descriptions of matter at the atomic scale. The magnesium comparison distinguishes a historical particle-on-path picture from a quantum orbital picture. Neutral magnesium has 12 electrons. The shell arrangement is 2–8–2, meaning two electrons in the first shell, eight in the second, and two in the third.

The listed ground-state configuration is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s². In the quantum picture, occupied wave modes contribute electron density rather than tracing tiny solar-system paths. The separate 1s², 2s², 2p⁶ and 3s² density illustrations are added to make the total electron density, and darker shading indicates greater density. The 2p⁶ contribution includes all three filled p orbitals.

The orbital thumbnails each use their own scale. Orbital sizes and density contrast are schematic, and the combined picture adds probability densities. Atomic orbitals are quantized wave modes, but magnesium itself is not a harmonic-oscillator atom. The shared use of wave ideas does not make the quantum picture identical to the classical shell drawing.
issues: The small original magnesium figure contains qualifications that narrow the slide’s broad harmonic-oscillator analogy. Those qualifications are retained.

sections.title: Two quantities in an oscillator
teaching: The equations ẋ = v and v̇ = −x describe position and velocity changing each other. A dot means change with time. Velocity determines the increase or decrease in position, while position determines the increase or decrease in velocity with the opposite sign.

The two arrows connect X and V in both directions. Positive x pushes velocity downward, which can make position fall. Negative x pushes velocity upward, which can make position rise. A moving system can therefore pass its resting position and be turned back from the other side.

sections.title: Repeated change in a loop
teaching: Oscillation is repeated back-and-forth change. The X-to-V arrow and the V-to-X arrow form a closed dynamical system. A change in one quantity changes the other, and that second change returns to affect the first.

The wavy trace alternates between high and low values across time. Repetition comes from the continuing interaction between the two quantities, rather than from independently issuing a new command for each turn.

sections.title: Why a spring and a mass make vibration
teaching: A spring provides a tendency to return toward a resting configuration. Stiffness describes how strongly it pushes back when displaced. Mass supplies the tendency of moving matter to keep moving. A spring can pull a mass toward the resting position, but the moving mass can continue through that position, so the spring must slow it and turn it back from the opposite side.

This interaction helps connect apparently different kinds of vibration. The examples include a car responding to a bump, music, economic boom and bust, oscillation during SGD, vibrating air in the vocal tract, and vibrating vocal folds during speech. The things moving differ, but repeated change and feedback are shared themes.

sections.title: Balancing feedback reduces displacement
teaching: The viscous-spring model ẋ = −⅓x makes the change oppose the current displacement. If x is positive, its rate is negative and x falls. If x is negative, its rate is positive and x rises. Both directions lead toward the same natural resting position at x = 0.

Starting from x = 1, the one-third factor makes the initial return relatively large. As the displacement becomes smaller, the magnitude of its rate of change becomes smaller too. The x-against-t curve therefore approaches zero steeply at first and then flattens. Starting below zero gives the opposite-looking curve, rising toward zero and flattening from below.

This is negative or balancing feedback because the system acts against the discrepancy from equilibrium. The motion reduces the very displacement that causes it. Once x is zero, the return-driving change is zero. In this model, making the magnitude of the restoring coefficient larger makes the return faster. A smaller magnitude gives a slower return.
issues: The source occasionally uses “ẋ will fall” where its intended question concerns the direction of x. The teaching distinguishes a quantity from its rate. The negative sign indicates direction, while the restoring strength is the coefficient’s magnitude.

sections.title: Mass carries motion onward
teaching: A mass in motion tends to stay in motion unless an influence changes that motion. The constant-velocity animation represents this by moving the rider the same distance during each equal interval, with an arrow pointing in the direction of travel. Position changes, but speed does not rise and fall in that demonstration.

The principle associated here with Galileo, Descartes and Newton explains why reaching a particular position does not automatically stop a moving mass. A return toward equilibrium can therefore continue past equilibrium when mass is part of the system.

sections.title: Returning to a place versus passing through it
teaching: Displacement x is measured from the spring’s natural position, marked x = 0. Pulling the spring alone to x = +1 stretches it, and releasing it makes the endpoint approach zero without crossing it. The blue x-against-t trace falls toward zero and gradually flattens.

Pushing the spring alone to x = −1 compresses it. After release, the endpoint approaches zero from the negative side. The red trace rises toward zero without crossing it. Both cases reduce the displacement rather than repeatedly changing its sign.

Attaching a mass changes the result. A mass released from x = +1 moves toward zero and continues through it because it is already moving. The spring is then compressed, so its pull reverses the change in velocity and eventually turns the mass back. The mass carries motion through the next crossing as well.

The orange trace is labelled lightly damped oscillation. It repeatedly crosses zero, with peaks and troughs becoming somewhat smaller. The contrast is between a direct approach to the natural position and a continuing process of overshooting and turning around. The natural position stays the same even though the motion around it changes.

sections.title: Frequency counts cycles in a fixed interval
teaching: The three air-slice models use the same particle-spacing range and all begin at maximum rarefaction. What changes is how many complete compression–rarefaction cycles fit into the same interval. The low-frequency example completes 3 cycles in 12 seconds, the middle example completes 6, and the high-frequency example completes 9.

Each graph plots normalized expansion x, from −1 to +1, against time from 0 to 12 seconds. The low-frequency curve has broad cycles. The middle curve fits twice as many cycles into that interval, and the high-frequency curve fits three times as many as the low-frequency curve. More cycles in the same time means higher frequency.

The moving points and particle diagrams remain synchronized within each panel. A value of +1 means maximum rarefaction, zero means equilibrium spacing, and −1 means maximum compression. Equal ranges do not imply equal frequencies. The particles can expand and contract by the same amount while completing the motion at different rates.

sections.title: Predict the effect of mass and stiffness
teaching: Perturbation theory asks how behavior changes when a system’s settings are changed. For a mass–spring system, increasing mass lowers the frequency. The same spring has more moving mass to slow and turn around, so each cycle takes longer and fewer cycles fit into a second.

Increasing stiffness raises the frequency. The stiffer spring returns the mass more strongly for the same displacement, so changes of direction happen more quickly and more cycles fit into a second. The two relationships are therefore m ↑ with f ↓, and k ↑ with f ↑. Mass and stiffness have opposite effects on frequency.

sections.title: Hearing separates a mixture into frequencies
teaching: Georg von Békésy received the Nobel Prize in 1961 for his work on hearing. The supplied hearing notes explain frequency separation through a basilar membrane whose mass and stiffness vary along its length.

The wide end is relatively heavy and loose, with larger mass and smaller stiffness, so both properties favor lower frequencies. The narrow end is relatively light and stiff, so both properties favor higher frequencies. Intermediate locations respond to intermediate frequencies. Which nerve fibers become active tells the brain where vibration is strongest and therefore which frequencies are present.
A mixture containing several frequencies can stimulate different locations. This physical separation helps the auditory system distinguish different frequency combinations in speech.

sections.title: Learning rate trades speed for steadiness
teaching: The learning rate γ determines how strongly each new observation changes the estimate. The four graphs place epochs from 0 to 300 on the horizontal axis and estimate x on the vertical axis. Red, green and blue runs begin near 130, 80 and 10, respectively, and approach the region around 80.

At a 1% learning rate, all three paths are smooth but the runs starting far from 80 still approach it slowly after 300 epochs. The 10% runs reach its neighborhood much sooner and then fluctuate only modestly. The 50% runs arrive quickly but keep making larger jumps around that region. At 80%, the estimate reacts very strongly to observations and keeps bouncing over a wide range.

Increasing γ gives faster movement toward the target region but less stable accuracy around it. Decreasing γ gives slower movement but smaller fluctuations. Oscillation in SGD is one example of a system continuing to change around a target.

Optimization seeks better ways to get both speed and accuracy. The aim is to improve the training method so that useful progress is fast without keeping the estimate widely scattered around its answer.

sections.title: Mass, stiffness and the frequencies of speech
teaching: Increasing the mass of a mass–spring system lowers its frequency, while increasing its stiffness raises its frequency. Greater mass takes longer to turn around under the same spring’s influence. Greater stiffness changes the motion more strongly and makes each cycle quicker.

Different tongue configurations alter where the air in the vocal tract is squeezed. The comparison includes high-front dean, high-back dune, low-front Dan, low-back Don and central done. Changing the shape changes the effective mass and stiffness of different portions of air, so the vibrating air contains a combination of frequencies that depends on the sound being produced.

Hearing speech therefore requires more than detecting that vibration exists. The auditory system must distinguish the lower, middle and higher frequency components and how strongly they are present. Different combinations help the listener distinguish speech examples such as scene and son.

sections.title: Frequency is represented by place and nerve activity
teaching: The cochlea converts a combination of sound frequencies into a pattern of neural activity. Different locations along the basilar membrane have different effective mass and stiffness. A heavier, looser location favors a lower frequency, while a lighter, stiffer location favors a higher frequency.

sections.title: How vocal folds make and change pitch
teaching: Vocal folds are small muscular structures, described here as about 1 cm long and 1 mm high. Muscle has both mass and stiffness. About ten other muscles acting through the surrounding bones and cartilages can stretch the folds and make them stiffer, or bunch them and make them effectively heavier.

Changing the fold properties changes how quickly they vibrate. Their vibration frequency is called F0 or the fundamental frequency, and is connected to pitch. Pitch control supports singing. In English it can convey a question, mistrust, degree of belief, surprise or emotion. In tone languages, pitch differences can distinguish word meanings.

Air taken into the lungs builds pressure below closed folds. Sufficient pressure pushes them apart and air flows between them. The pressure-and-airflow account connects the subsequent inward movement to suction, compared with a shower curtain being drawn inward. Closure allows pressure to build again, opening the folds again. Repetition hundreds of times per second creates vibration.

The account names the suction effect the Bernoulli force and connects it with the familiar airplane example. The vibrating folds are tissue, while the air moving through and above them is a different physical part of speech production.

sections.title: Position-first updates keep the oscillator bounded
teaching: The oscillator uses ẋ = v and v̇ = −(k/m)x with k/m = 1, a time step Δt = 0.5, and the starting state x = 1, v = 0. Position is updated first using the old velocity. Velocity is then updated using the newly calculated position. The order matters because the second calculation receives information from the first.

The first step keeps x at 1.000 because the old velocity is zero, while velocity becomes −0.500. The next position becomes 0.750, and the updated velocity becomes −0.875. As position crosses to the negative side, the restoring change in velocity becomes positive, eventually reversing the direction of motion.

The displayed x sequence is [1, 1.000, 0.750, 0.313, −0.203, −0.668, −0.966, −1.022, −0.823, −0.418, 0.091, 0.578, 0.920]. The corresponding v sequence is [0, −0.500, −0.875, −1.031, −0.930, −0.596, −0.113, 0.398, 0.810, 1.019, 0.973, 0.684, 0.224]. Each pair supplies one plotted state in the x-against-time and v-against-time graphs.

These approximate numerical values stay within a limited range while alternating in sign. They are not exact cosine and sine samples. The procedure is position-first symplectic Euler, and later steps use full precision even though the labels are rounded to three decimal places. The growing lists store the sequence of successive states.

sections.title: Explicit Euler uses the old pair for both updates
teaching: Explicit Euler starts from x[0] = 1 and v[0] = 0, with k = 1, m = 1 and dt = 0.5. Its position update is x[n] = v[n−1] × dt + x[n−1]. Its velocity update is v[n] = −(k/m)x[n−1] × dt + v[n−1]. Both calculations use the previous pair, so the velocity update does not use the newly calculated position.

The first step gives x = 1.000 and v = −0.500. The second gives x = 0.750 and v = −1.000. Position and velocity then continue changing signs, but their excursion becomes progressively larger rather than staying near the original range.

The x list is [1, 1.000, 0.750, 0.250, −0.438, −1.188, −1.828, −2.172, −2.059, −1.402, −0.231, 1.290, 2.869]. The v list is [0, −0.500, −1.000, −1.375, −1.500, −1.281, −0.688, 0.227, 1.313, 2.342, 3.043, 3.159, 2.514]. The graphs plot these values against time. The final displayed arithmetic uses the previous position 1.290 and velocity 3.159 to obtain the next position 2.869 and velocity 2.514 after rounding.

The growing amplitude comes from this numerical approximation with the stated time step. It is not evidence that the intended undamped physical oscillator spontaneously gains larger and larger motion. Changing which version of a state an update uses can change the behavior of the numerical simulation.

sections.title: Differential equations express how systems change
teaching: A differential equation describes relationships involving rates of change. It therefore provides a mathematical expression of a dynamical system, in which the current quantities determine how the system changes with time. The lecture connects that perspective with physical processes, inference and learning.

The expanded Latin statement is “Data aequatione quotcunque fluentes quantitates involvente fluxiones invenire, et vice versa”.

The supplied paraphrase, attributed to Vladimir Arnold, is that the laws of nature are expressed by differential equations. The relevant connection is between knowing the relationships that govern change and predicting how a system evolves. The same broad dynamical perspective motivates the lecture’s connection to learning and inference in LLMs.

sections.title: Predict a return toward equilibrium step by step
teaching: The equation ẋ = −⅓x makes the rate of change oppose the current value. An initial condition supplies where the process begins. sections.title: A signal becomes a distribution over identities
teaching: A neural network takes a signal represented by numbers and returns a distribution over possible identities. sections.title: Learning changes the weights after an error
teaching: A speech input can be a vector such as [4, 1, −3, 2, 1, 0.4, 1, 2, −3, …], representing pressure values from a waveform. Such input values can be positive or negative. They are not probabilities. The output instead distributes probability among the possible vowel identities.

The network’s learned knowledge resides in numerical weights w. Combining the signal with those weights through many calculations gives an output decision. The weights are not supplied by already knowing the correct answer. Training can begin with random weights and improve them from mistakes, the “fake it till you make it” idea.

For an input whose correct identity is the vowel in Rud, the initial forward propagation produces [0.4, 0.1, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1]. That output gives the largest probability to read rather than Rud. The known target is [0, 0, 0, 1, 0], with all target probability on the fourth category. Comparing the computed output with the target gives an error or loss.

Training changes the weights to reduce that loss, then repeats the process with another labelled signal. Large systems can involve very many weights and calculations, with the lecture using trillions of weights and billions of training repetitions to convey the possible scale. The repeated learning procedure is separate from the act of computing one output with the current weights.

sections.title: Template matching and successive representations
teaching: A speech recognizer receiving a [z] pressure waveform should identify [z] rather than [s] or [a]. The decision requires a way to compare the incoming signal with learned information. Two ideas from animal perception help organize that problem, template matching and hierarchical processing.

Template matching compares an input with stored internal patterns. Hierarchical processing turns an input into a new representation, then transforms that representation again through further stages. An artificial neural network can combine these ideas by comparing numerical patterns at several successive levels.

sections.title: Templates make familiarity into a comparison
teaching: In the templatic theory of face perception, light information from a face reaches the retina. The brain has stored internal templates for familiar faces. It compares the incoming face with each template, and the template with the greatest similarity determines which face is perceived. If a name is associated with that winning template, the name becomes the identification.

For the neural-network analogy, weights serve as numerical templates. Combining an input with the weights is a way to evaluate how the incoming pattern matches the internal patterns. Before learning, the templates are poor and the computed answer can be wrong. Training changes the templates so that the comparison becomes more useful.

sections.title: Perception involves connected stages

sections.title: An inner product compares two numerical patterns
teaching: Template matching requires a way to compare lists of numbers. Here the input is [−1, 3, −2], the first template is [−2, 0, 3], and the second template is [−2, 2, −1]. An inner product multiplies corresponding entries and then adds the products.

For the first template, the positive contribution from the first pair is outweighed by the negative contribution from the final pair, while the middle pair contributes zero. The result is −4. For the second template, all three contributions are positive and the result is 10. The second template therefore receives the larger positive match in this example.

The comparison rule treats an inner product near zero as little match and a large positive inner product as stronger match. It is the stated template score for this example. The weights and the input have the same number of components so that their entries can be paired.

sections.title: Inference uses weights and learning improves them
teaching: Inference begins with a signal vector and uses the current weights to compute an identity or distribution. Inner products provide repeated template comparisons. A result at one level becomes the input for another level, giving the hierarchy of representations.

Learning begins with an input whose correct identity is known. The network first performs inference using its current weights. If initially random weights give a poor answer, the mismatch provides a loss and SGD improves the weights. Inference is therefore part of a learning step, but changing weights is what makes the step learning.

The comparison with Euler’s algorithm concerns building a result through repeated simple computations. Repeating an operation across stages can produce a complex behavior even when each individual operation is arithmetic.

sections.title: A receiving neuron combines weighted inputs
teaching: Cajal’s retinal circuit represents a brain made of connected neurons. The circles identify neuronal cell bodies. Signals pass through selected contacts toward receiving neurons, and those contacts are represented by synaptic weights in the arithmetic model.

An activation is the signal value associated with a unit. A synaptic weight represents how strongly an incoming activation affects the receiving unit. Positive and negative weights allow different contributions to reinforce or oppose one another. Signals pass through connected contacts, and the arithmetic abstraction replaces each selected contact with its own signed weight. Three inputs then converge on one receiving neuron.

The input activations are −1, 1 and 3, and their weights are −2, 3 and 1. The receiving neuron multiplies each activation by its own weight and adds the contributions. The displayed computation is (−1 × −2) + (1 × 3) + (3 × 1) = 8. The same operation is called an inner product, scalar product or dot product. This example has no bias term.

The schematic signed numbers belong to an artificial-neuron model. A negative activation in that arithmetic example is not a claim that a biological neuron has a negative firing rate. The original retinal drawing is credited to Santiago Ramón y Cajal’s Recuerdos de mi vida, volume II, 1917, figure 40, with the image cropped and rotated to orient the depicted flow.

sections.title: Forward propagation through a multilayer perceptron
teaching: The multilayer perceptron has 5 input units, then hidden layers of 3, 4 and 3 units, and finally 7 output units. Every unit in one layer connects to every unit in the next layer. The 60 connections between adjacent layers each carry a weight that changes how strongly one activation contributes to another.

The first displayed set of five weights converges on the middle unit in Hidden 1. Its weights, from top input to bottom input, are [2, −1, 1, 3, −2]. With inputs [2, 1, 3, 4, 2], the contributions combine to give that unit an activation of 14. Negative weights can oppose positive contributions, so the activation is a weighted combination rather than a simple count of active inputs.

The ordered computation produces Hidden 1 activations [4, 14, −3]. These become inputs to Hidden 2, whose activations are [6, −2, 5, 1]. Hidden 3 then contains [3, −1, 2]. Each layer therefore creates a new representation from the current activations and its own connection weights.

The final softmax output is [0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.15, 0.12, 0.08]. These seven nonnegative values sum to 1.00. The fourth output is largest at 0.30, so it is the most supported category in this example. Negative hidden activations are allowed in the arithmetic, while output probabilities are nonnegative.

The demonstration uses linear hidden activations and no biases. The input activations appear first, then Hidden 1, Hidden 2 and Hidden 3 are computed in order, and the probabilities appear last. Forward propagation is this movement of computation from the input toward the output using the current weights.

sections.title: Use an output error to improve the weights
teaching: Training begins with random weights and an input whose correct output identity is known. In the stated training pair, the input is [−2, 1, 3, −4, 2] and the target is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0]. The sixth position identifies the correct output category.

The displayed computed distribution is [0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.15, 0.12, 0.08]. It puts only 0.12 on the correct sixth category and puts its highest probability, 0.30, on the fourth. Comparing this output with the known target gives the error that training should reduce.

Backpropagation carries information about the output error back through the layers so that the weights can be adjusted using SGD. Improving the weights changes the computed distribution on subsequent passes. Repeating prediction, comparison and adjustment across many input–output pairs builds the network’s learned knowledge.

The example emphasizes the scale of repetition in data centers, potentially billions of labelled input–output pairs. Inference computes with the weights currently available, while training uses known identities to improve those weights.

Backpropagation supplies the error derivatives used for an SGD update rather than being merely another name for SGD.

sections.title: An erroneous observation changes what gets learned
teaching: The average-estimation example uses [73, 90, 98, 46, 400, 81, 82, 78, 62, 91, 61, 84, 75, 84, 81, 75]. The value 400 is identified as a data mistake. Including it makes the list’s average about 100, while excluding it leaves an average about 80.

An update based on 400 pulls the estimate toward that unusually large value. Repeated learning can therefore fit the supplied data while moving away from the intended quantity if the observations themselves contain errors. Accurate arithmetic does not repair an incorrect observation automatically.

The demonstration treats the listed order as the order in which observations are encountered. The heading promises Python, but the supplied page contains the data and conceptual problem rather than an actual program.
